items.stem: Which term describes a group sharing a cultural identity based on factors such as language, religion, history and traditions?
items.answer: Ethnic group
items.markingKey: Ethnic group: a group sharing a cultural identity based on factors such as language, religion, history and traditions. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “exclusion”? Give one example.
items.answer: The removal of a pupil from school, temporarily or permanently, for disciplinary reasons. Example: a pupil expelled for repeated disruption.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the removal of a pupil from school, temporarily or permanently, for disciplinary reasons); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a pupil expelled for repeated disruption. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “exclusion” and “aspiration”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Exclusion: the removal of a pupil from school, temporarily or permanently, for disciplinary reasons (e.g. a pupil expelled for repeated disruption). Aspiration: hopes and ambitions for the future, such as going to university (e.g. parents expecting their children to become doctors).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Exam data from Mumbai show that pupils from one migrant community achieve well above the national average, while pupils from another achieve well below it. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: differences reflect cultural values and family support for education; schools should help all groups integrate into shared values (cultural deprivation view).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In Manila, black Caribbean boys are three times more likely to be excluded from school than the average pupil. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: differences reflect cultural values and family support for education; schools should help all groups integrate into shared values (cultural deprivation view).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful covert participant observation is for studying minority ethnic pupils’ experiences of school.
items.answer: Strengths: because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided; it can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher. Limitations: secretly recording sensitive behaviour without consent raises serious ethical problems of deception and harm; the researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying minority ethnic pupils’ experiences of school but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a group sharing a cultural identity based on factors such as language, religion, history and traditions?
items.answer: Ethnic group
items.markingKey: Ethnic group: a group sharing a cultural identity based on factors such as language, religion, history and traditions. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “intersectionality”.
items.answer: The way ethnicity combines with class and gender to shape outcomes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the way ethnicity combines with class and gender to shape outcomes. [1]

items.stem: A research team is investigating ethnic differences in exam results in Toronto. Explain one limitation of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: Being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of ethnic differences in exam results in Toronto. [2]

items.stem: Exam data from Seoul show that pupils from one migrant community achieve well above the national average, while pupils from another achieve well below it. Explain how interactionist and functionalist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: ethnic differences are partly created in schools through teachers’ stereotypes and labels, which shape set placements and pupils’ self-concepts (Archer, Gillborn). Functionalism: differences reflect cultural values and family support for education; schools should help all groups integrate into shared values (cultural deprivation view).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: National data for Bangkok (200 pupils) show exam results by ethnic group and eligibility for free school meals. Table: percentage achieving five good passes | Not eligible for free meals | Eligible for free meals. Group A | 74% | 62%. Group B | 57% | 47%. Group C | 60% | 55%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Not eligible for free meals and Eligible for free meals for Group A. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that class is more important than ethnicity in explaining differences in achievement.
items.answer: (a) 62 − 74 = -12 percentage points (Eligible for free meals compared with Not eligible for free meals). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Eligible for free meals than for Not eligible for free meals among Group A, Group B, Group C; Group A had the highest figure for Eligible for free meals. Teacher labelling and institutional racism may affect some groups more. Qualifications: Differences between ethnic groups remain even within the same poverty category; broad categories hide variation; official data do not show processes inside schools. The data also come from official statistics of 200 pupils aged 16 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 74 and 62; 1 mark for 12 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the theory that some groups lack the values, attitudes or skills needed for success in education?
items.answer: Cultural deprivation
items.markingKey: Cultural deprivation: the theory that some groups lack the values, attitudes or skills needed for success in education. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “material deprivation”, and give one example.
items.answer: Lack of money and resources that affect education, such as poor housing and diet. Example: a family in overcrowded housing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (lack of money and resources that affect education, such as poor housing and diet); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a family in overcrowded housing. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “linguistic deprivation” and “cultural deprivation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Linguistic deprivation: the theory that some children lack the language skills needed for school, for example if English is not their first language (e.g. a child struggling with exam language). Cultural deprivation: the theory that some groups lack the values, attitudes or skills needed for success in education (e.g. claims that some families do not value education).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In Hanoi, a migrant community runs Saturday schools where children study mathematics and their parents’ language. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: achievement reflects how far family cultures prepare children for school values; cultural deprivation can be overcome through compensatory education.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A family recently arrived in Jakarta live in a small flat; the parents, both qualified teachers in their home country, work as cleaners because their qualifications are not recognised. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: material deprivation, shaped by racism in the labour and housing markets, explains much underachievement; cultural explanations blame the victim.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Singapore wants to research the role of supplementary schools in minority communities. Evaluate the use of semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; a core set of questions allows some comparison between interviewees while follow-up questions add depth. Limitations: samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited; interviewer bias may still affect answers. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the role of supplementary schools in minority communities but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “supplementary school”.
items.answer: An out-of-school-hours school run by a community, often teaching language, culture or extra subjects.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: an out-of-school-hours school run by a community, often teaching language, culture or extra subjects. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “linguistic deprivation” and “racism in wider society”.
items.answer: Linguistic deprivation: the theory that some children lack the language skills needed for school, for example if English is not their first language. Racism in wider society: discrimination in areas such as jobs and housing that affects minority families’ resources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the experiences of pupils learning English as an additional language. Explain one limitation of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: The researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the experiences of pupils learning English as an additional language. [2]

items.stem: In Kathmandu, a migrant community runs Saturday schools where children study mathematics and their parents’ language. Compare how Marxist and New Right sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: material deprivation, shaped by racism in the labour and housing markets, explains much underachievement; cultural explanations blame the victim. New Right: family structure and culture explain underachievement: lack of father figures and anti-school street culture harm some boys (Sewell).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes discrimination built into the policies and practices of organisations, whether intended or not?
items.answer: Institutional racism
items.markingKey: Institutional racism: discrimination built into the policies and practices of organisations, whether intended or not. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “pupil identity”, and give one example.
items.answer: How teachers and others see a pupil, such as ideal, pathologised or demonised. Example: a pupil seen as a hard-working “model minority”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (how teachers and others see a pupil, such as ideal, pathologised or demonised); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a pupil seen as a hard-working “model minority”. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “racialised expectations” and “institutional racism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Racialised expectations: teachers’ assumptions about pupils’ ability or behaviour based on ethnicity (e.g. expecting black pupils to be disruptive). Institutional racism: discrimination built into the policies and practices of organisations, whether intended or not (e.g. set placement systems that place disproportionate numbers of black pupils in lower sets).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: The history syllabus in Singapore covers the nation’s kings and wars but says almost nothing about the countries from which many pupils’ families came. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: teachers’ racialised expectations and labels affect pupils’ treatment and self-concept; some pupils accept labels while others resist (Wright, Fuller).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In a school in Mumbai, pupils from one minority group make up 10% of the school but 30% of exclusions. Explain how a neo-Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: critical race theorists argue racism is built into school structures such as assessment, setting and the curriculum, locking in inequality (Gillborn).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: In a school in Kathmandu, pupils from one minority group make up 10% of the school but 30% of exclusions. Explain how functionalist and interactionist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: schools should promote shared national values and integration; differences in outcomes reflect cultural and family factors rather than school practices. Interactionism: teachers’ racialised expectations and labels affect pupils’ treatment and self-concept; some pupils accept labels while others resist (Wright, Fuller).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of case studies for studying teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups.
items.answer: Strengths: they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community; they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples. Limitations: the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases; the researcher’s interpretation may be biased. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Kwame, a sociology student, is designing a project on the content of the school history curriculum. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable; it is cheap and the sources (newspapers, television, websites) are easy to obtain. Limitations: counting does not reveal the meanings audiences take from the content; coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the content of the school history curriculum but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a curriculum that reflects the culture of one ethnic group, usually the majority, and marginalises others?
items.answer: Ethnocentric curriculum
items.markingKey: Ethnocentric curriculum: a curriculum that reflects the culture of one ethnic group, usually the majority, and marginalises others. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “locked-in inequality”.
items.answer: Gillborn’s idea that racial inequality is so deeply rooted that it is built into the system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: Gillborn’s idea that racial inequality is so deeply rooted that it is built into the system. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “pupil identity” and “locked-in inequality”?
items.answer: Pupil identity: how teachers and others see a pupil, such as ideal, pathologised or demonised. Locked-in inequality: Gillborn’s idea that racial inequality is so deeply rooted that it is built into the system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Official data for schools in Kathmandu (about 10000 pupils) show exclusion rates by ethnic group. Table: permanent and fixed-term exclusions per 1,000 pupils | 2015 | 2025. Group A | 29 | 31. Group B | 10 | 8. All pupils | 14 | 16. By how many exclusions per 1,000 pupils did the figure for All pupils change between 2015 and 2025?
items.answer: +2 exclusions per 1,000 pupils
items.markingKey: 16 − 14 = +2 exclusions per 1,000 pupils. [1]

items.stem: Official data for schools in Nairobi (about 10000 pupils) show exclusion rates by ethnic group. Table: permanent and fixed-term exclusions per 1,000 pupils | 2015 | 2025. Group A | 29 | 32. Group B | 12 | 13. All pupils | 15 | 15. (a) Calculate the change, in exclusions per 1,000 pupils, for Group A between 2015 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that institutional racism explains ethnic differences in exclusions.
items.answer: (a) 32 − 29 = +3 exclusions per 1,000 pupils. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Group A, Group B; Group A had the highest figure for 2025. Material deprivation linked to behaviour difficulties. Qualifications: Exclusion rates may also reflect differences in class and family circumstances; statistics do not show the reasons for each exclusion; rates differ between schools. The data also come from official statistics of 1000 pupils in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 29 and 32; 1 mark for +3 exclusions per 1,000 pupils (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Official data for schools in Accra (about 2400 pupils) show exclusion rates by ethnic group. Table: permanent and fixed-term exclusions per 1,000 pupils | 2015 | 2025. Group A | 30 | 29. Group B | 8 | 9. All pupils | 10 | 13. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Group A between 2015 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that institutional racism explains ethnic differences in exclusions.
items.answer: (a) (29 − 30) ÷ 30 × 100 = -3.3%. (b) Definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Group B, All pupils; the figure fell for Group A; Group A had the highest figure for 2025. Institutional racism in behaviour policies. Qualifications: Exclusion rates may also reflect differences in class and family circumstances; statistics do not show the reasons for each exclusion; rates differ between schools. The data also come from official statistics of 240 pupils in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (29 − 30) ÷ 30 × 100; 1 mark for -3.3% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the difference in average results between groups?
items.answer: Attainment gap
items.markingKey: Attainment gap: the difference in average results between groups. [1]

items.stem: State one reason why some ethnic minority groups achieve above the national average.
items.answer: Education seen as a route out of disadvantage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. education seen as a route out of disadvantage. [1]

items.stem: Modood argued that ethnic minority groups have high aspirations and many achieve well despite disadvantage. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Modood found many ethnic minority families valued education highly, and some groups outperformed the majority despite lower incomes. Criticism: Aggregated categories can hide large differences within ethnic groups.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows results for 600 pupils in Mumbai, by ethnic group and poverty. Table: percentage achieving five good passes | Not eligible for free meals | Eligible for free meals. Group A | 77% | 71%. Group B | 56% | 38%. Group C | 64% | 56%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Not eligible for free meals and Eligible for free meals for Group A (Eligible for free meals minus Not eligible for free meals)?
items.answer: -6 percentage points
items.markingKey: 71 − 77 = -6 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Tariq is planning a study of ethnic differences in exam results in Toronto. Explain two limitations of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. The interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. 2. The fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to ethnic differences in exam results in Toronto. [4]

items.stem: Explain two patterns of ethnic differences in educational achievement.
items.answer: Some groups above and some below average; gender gaps within groups; class effects within groups; exclusion rates; differences in university entry.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Some groups above and some below average; gender gaps within groups; class effects within groups; exclusion rates; differences in university entry. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the theory that some children lack the language skills needed for school, for example if English is not their first language?
items.answer: Linguistic deprivation
items.markingKey: Linguistic deprivation: the theory that some children lack the language skills needed for school, for example if English is not their first language. [1]

items.stem: Outline what Lupton meant by arguing that respect for adult authority in some families encourages good behaviour in school.
items.answer: Lupton found that adult authority in Indian and Chinese families paralleled school authority, which helped pupils’ behaviour and achievement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Lupton found that adult authority in Indian and Chinese families paralleled school authority, which helped pupils’ behaviour and achievement. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “linguistic deprivation” and “racism in wider society”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Linguistic deprivation: the theory that some children lack the language skills needed for school, for example if English is not their first language (e.g. a child struggling with exam language). Racism in wider society: discrimination in areas such as jobs and housing that affects minority families’ resources (e.g. parents denied jobs because of ethnicity).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Omar, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on ethnicity and income in Kuala Lumpur. The report was based on 400 households with children. Table: percentage of households in relative poverty | 2010 | 2025. Group A | 45% | 41%. Group B | 28% | 24%. Majority group | 21% | 18%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Group A change between 2010 and 2025?
items.answer: -4 percentage points
items.markingKey: 41 − 45 = -4 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Grace is planning a study of the role of supplementary schools in minority communities. Explain two limitations of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. They are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. 2. The interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the role of supplementary schools in minority communities. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful field experiments are for studying the experiences of pupils learning English as an additional language.
items.answer: Strengths: variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom; one variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect. Limitations: they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change; participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of pupils learning English as an additional language but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes discrimination built into the policies and practices of organisations, whether intended or not?
items.answer: Institutional racism
items.markingKey: Institutional racism: discrimination built into the policies and practices of organisations, whether intended or not. [1]

items.stem: State one feature of an ethnocentric curriculum.
items.answer: Literature drawn mainly from one culture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. literature drawn mainly from one culture. [1]

items.stem: Fuller argued that black girls can reject negative labels and succeed. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Fuller studied black girls in a London school who worked hard to prove teachers wrong while appearing anti-school to peers. Criticism: Not all pupils have the resources to resist labels.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Lina, a sociology student, is designing a project on teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups. Explain one limitation of using case studies for this research.
items.answer: One case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups. [2]

items.stem: Official data for schools in Riyadh (about 10000 pupils) show exclusion rates by ethnic group. Table: permanent and fixed-term exclusions per 1,000 pupils | 2015 | 2025. Group A | 34 | 27. Group B | 14 | 11. All pupils | 10 | 8. By how many exclusions per 1,000 pupils did the figure for Group B change between 2015 and 2025?
items.answer: -3 exclusions per 1,000 pupils
items.markingKey: 11 − 14 = -3 exclusions per 1,000 pupils. [1]

items.stem: Official data for schools in Auckland (about 8000 pupils) show exclusion rates by ethnic group. Table: permanent and fixed-term exclusions per 1,000 pupils | 2015 | 2025. Group A | 35 | 36. Group B | 11 | 11. All pupils | 14 | 14. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for All pupils between 2015 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Calculate the gap between All pupils and Group B in 2015 and in 2025, and state whether it narrowed or widened.
items.answer: (a) (14 − 14) ÷ 14 × 100 = 0%. (b) 2015: 3 exclusions per 1,000 pupils; 2025: 3 exclusions per 1,000 pupils; the gap stayed the same.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (14 − 14) ÷ 14 × 100; 1 mark for 0% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark each gap (3 and 3); 1 mark for “stayed the same”. [3]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which schools may contribute to ethnic differences in achievement.
items.answer: Labelling and racialised expectations (Wright); setting and assessment (Gillborn); ethnocentric curriculum (Coard); exclusions; pupil identities (Archer).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Labelling and racialised expectations (Wright); setting and assessment (Gillborn); ethnocentric curriculum (Coard); exclusions; pupil identities (Archer). [8]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using case studies to research teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups.
items.answer: Strengths: they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples; they may use several methods, increasing validity. Limitations: the researcher’s interpretation may be biased; one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the way ethnicity combines with class and gender to shape outcomes?
items.answer: Intersectionality
items.markingKey: Intersectionality: the way ethnicity combines with class and gender to shape outcomes. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “ethnic group”?
items.answer: A group sharing a cultural identity based on factors such as language, religion, history and traditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a group sharing a cultural identity based on factors such as language, religion, history and traditions. [1]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why official statistics on ethnicity and achievement should be treated with caution.
items.answer: Ethnic categories are broad and hide differences (e.g. between national origins); self-classification varies; class and gender are not always controlled; changes in categories over time; small group sizes.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained reason. [4]

items.stem: The table shows results for 240 pupils in Bogotá, by ethnic group and poverty. Table: percentage achieving five good passes | Not eligible for free meals | Eligible for free meals. Group A | 78% | 73%. Group B | 53% | 36%. Group C | 70% | 56%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Not eligible for free meals and Eligible for free meals for Group C (Eligible for free meals minus Not eligible for free meals)?
items.answer: -14 percentage points
items.markingKey: 56 − 70 = -14 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Exam data from Kuala Lumpur show that pupils from one migrant community achieve well above the national average, while pupils from another achieve well below it. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: ethnic differences are bound up with class inequality: minority groups are over-represented in poverty and institutional racism helps reproduce disadvantage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) to research ethnic differences in exam results in Santiago.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they show how people’s lives change over time and allow cause and effect to be explored. Limitations: they are very expensive and results take many years to appear; sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying ethnic differences in exam results in Santiago but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes lack of money and resources that affect education, such as poor housing and diet?
items.answer: Material deprivation
items.markingKey: Material deprivation: lack of money and resources that affect education, such as poor housing and diet. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Pupils who speak English as an additional language always underachieve.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many EAL pupils catch up and achieve well; language is not a long-term barrier for most.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain Lupton’s argument that respect for adult authority in some families encourages good behaviour in school, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Lupton found that adult authority in Indian and Chinese families paralleled school authority, which helped pupils’ behaviour and achievement. Criticism: This may reinforce stereotypes about particular groups.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Functionalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Felix, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on ethnicity and income in Manila. The report was based on 600 households with children. Table: percentage of households in relative poverty | 2010 | 2025. Group A | 44% | 42%. Group B | 30% | 33%. Majority group | 21% | 20%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Majority group change between 2010 and 2025?
items.answer: -1 percentage point
items.markingKey: 20 − 21 = -1 percentage point. [1]

items.stem: In Kuala Lumpur, a migrant community runs Saturday schools where children study mathematics and their parents’ language. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: achievement reflects how far family cultures prepare children for school values; cultural deprivation can be overcome through compensatory education.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Nadia, a sociology student, is designing a project on the experiences of pupils learning English as an additional language. Evaluate the use of covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it produces rich, first-hand qualitative data with high validity; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: studying children covertly is ethically unacceptable because they cannot consent and are vulnerable; the study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of pupils learning English as an additional language but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a curriculum that reflects the culture of one ethnic group, usually the majority, and marginalises others?
items.answer: Ethnocentric curriculum
items.markingKey: Ethnocentric curriculum: a curriculum that reflects the culture of one ethnic group, usually the majority, and marginalises others. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “ethnocentric curriculum”.
items.answer: A curriculum that reflects the culture of one ethnic group, usually the majority, and marginalises others.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a curriculum that reflects the culture of one ethnic group, usually the majority, and marginalises others. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which teachers’ labels may affect minority ethnic pupils.
items.answer: Racialised expectations lead to harsher discipline and exclusion; lower set and tier placements; self-fulfilling prophecy; pupils may form subcultures or resist (Fuller); some groups positively stereotyped (Archer).
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: The history syllabus in Manila covers the nation’s kings and wars but says almost nothing about the countries from which many pupils’ families came. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: teachers’ racialised expectations and labels affect pupils’ treatment and self-concept; some pupils accept labels while others resist (Wright, Fuller).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Official data for schools in Karachi (about 5000 pupils) show exclusion rates by ethnic group. Table: permanent and fixed-term exclusions per 1,000 pupils | 2015 | 2025. Group A | 27 | 28. Group B | 11 | 10. All pupils | 12 | 15. By how many exclusions per 1,000 pupils did the figure for Group A change between 2015 and 2025?
items.answer: +1 exclusions per 1,000 pupil
items.markingKey: 28 − 27 = +1 exclusions per 1,000 pupil. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Nairobi wants to research the content of the school history curriculum. Explain one strength of using content analysis for this research.
items.answer: It is cheap and the sources (newspapers, television, websites) are easy to obtain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the content of the school history curriculum. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of semi-structured interviews for studying the content of the school history curriculum.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; a core set of questions allows some comparison between interviewees while follow-up questions add depth. Limitations: samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited; follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the content of the school history curriculum but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups.
items.answer: Strengths: anonymity may encourage respondents to admit sensitive or embarrassing behaviour they would not reveal face to face; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying teachers’ expectations of pupils from different ethnic groups but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
